title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple

revision.summary: Practice Present Perfect vs Past Simple.

body_content:
Practice Present Perfect vs Past Simple.

Say it: have and has

In the present perfect have and has are weak: I've been /aɪv biːn/, she's seen. Stress the past participle: I've SEEN it.

Where accents differ

UKHave you eaten yet?
I've already had lunch.
been /biːn/
USDid you eat yet? (also common)
I already had lunch.
been /bɪn/
Say it: "I've lived here for years. She's never been to Rome."

audio_urls.title: Say it: have / has in the present perfect

title: Second Conditional
body_content:
Practice Second Conditional.

Say it: would

In the second conditional would is short: I'd /aɪd/, she'd. Stress the idea: If I had more TIME, I'd TRAVEL. A rise on the if-clause and a fall at the end sound natural.

Say it: "If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house."

title: Reported Speech
body_content:
Practice Reported Speech.

Listen for: reported speech

In speech reporting verbs are quick and the reported words carry the stress: She said she was TIRED. He told me he'd CALL. Listen for said, told, asked, then the stressed content.

Listen: who said it, and what was the main news?

title: Passive Voice
body_content:
Practice Passive Voice.

Say it: passive voice

In passives the auxiliary is weak and the participle is stressed: It was BUILT in 1990. English is SPOKEN here. Was is /wəz/ and were is /wə/.

Say it: "The bridge was built in 1990. These cars are made in Spain."

title: First vs Second Conditional (Contrast)
body_content:
Practice First vs Second Conditional (Contrast).

Say it: contrast stress

To contrast two ideas, stress the different word: If I HAVE time, I'll go. If I HAD time, I'd go. Say the contrasting words louder and longer.

Say it: "If it rains, we'll stay. If it rained, we'd stay."

revision.summary: Practice Adverbs of Manner and Modifiers.

title: Present Perfect Continuous
body_content:
Practice Present Perfect Continuous.

Say it: been

In have been the word been is weak. Keep the stress on the -ing verb: I've been WAITing for an hour.

Where accents differ

UKbeen /biːn/ (strong) or /bɪn/ (weak)
USbeen /bɪn/
Say it: "I've been working here since May."

revision.summary: Practice Look + adjective, look like + noun.

title: Be able to / can / manage to

revision.summary: Practice Be able to / can / manage to.

title: Past Perfect Simple
body_content:
Practice Past Perfect Simple.

Say it: had

In the past perfect had is short: She'd left /ʃiːd left/, they'd arrived. Do not stress had. Stress the participle: I'd already LEFT.

Say it: "When I arrived, the film had started."

title: Be allowed to and be supposed to

revision.summary: Practice Be allowed to and be supposed to.
Practice A few and a little.

title: Although / in spite of / despite

revision.summary: Practice Although / in spite of / despite.

body_content:
Practice Although / in spite of / despite.

Say it: linking contrast

After a contrast word, pause for a short chunk boundary: Although it was late, | we went out. Use a fall on the first chunk and a fall at the end.

Say it: "Despite the rain, we had a great time."

title: Question tags
body_content:
Practice Question tags.

Say it: question tags

With a falling tag you expect agreement: It's cold, isn't it? ↘ With a rising tag you are really asking: You're coming, aren't you? ↗ The intonation changes the meaning.

Where accents differ

UKIt's lovely, isn't it? is very common
USIt's nice, right? is common and informal
Say it: "It's a nice day, isn't it?" (agree) / "You're coming, aren't you?" (ask)

title: Clothes
body_content:
Practice Clothes.

Listen for: clothes words

Clothes words differ between British and American English. Listen for both in shops and films.

Where accents differ

UKjumper, trousers, trainers
waistcoat
USsweater, pants, sneakers
vest
Listen: which word does the speaker use for trousers?

title: Holidays and travel brochures
body_content:
Practice Holidays and travel brochures.

Listen for: holiday words

Holiday and travel words differ. Listen for both when you read brochures or listen to announcements.

Where accents differ

UKholiday
flat
luggage
USvacation
apartment
baggage
Listen: which word does the speaker use, holiday or vacation?

title: Furniture and appliances
body_content:
Practice Furniture and appliances.

Listen for: home appliances

Home words differ between accents. Learn both so you understand instructions and adverts.

Where accents differ

UKcooker
hoover (vacuum cleaner)
tap
USstove
vacuum
faucet
Listen: which word does the speaker use for tap?

title: Types of books, films, and TV programmes

revision.summary: Practice Types of books, films, and TV programmes.

title: Political Systems
body_content:
Practice Political Systems.

Say it: word stress

Long words have one main stress: deMOcracy, goVERNment, ELection, poliTIcian. Stress shifts in related words: POLitics but poLITical.

Say it: "democracy, government, election, politician."

audio_urls.title: Say it: word stress in politics

title: Describing location of people and things

revision.summary: Practice Describing location of people and things.

title: Stating preferences and opinions
body_content:
Practice Stating preferences and opinions.

Say it: opinions

Softening an opinion needs gentle stress and a fall-rise: I'm not SURE that's right. In my OPINion... I THINK so. Stress the opinion word, not I.

Say it: "I prefer tea to coffee. In my opinion, it's better."

title: Advising
body_content:
Practice Advising.

Say it: giving advice

Advice sounds kind with a falling voice and a soft tone: You should REST. Why don't you TRY it? If I were YOU, I'd... A rising tone can sound unsure.

Say it: "You should see a doctor. If I were you, I'd wait."

title: Talking about possibility / probability and certainty

revision.summary: Practice Talking about possibility / probability and certainty.

title: Refusing
body_content:
Practice Refusing.

Say it: refusing politely

Soften a refusal with a fall-rise and a warm tone: I'm afraid I can't. ↘↗ That's very kind, but no, thanks. A flat, fast No. can sound rude.

Where accents differ

UKI'm afraid I can't /kɑːnt/
USI'm afraid I can't /kænt/ (a shorter vowel)
Say it: "I'm afraid I can't come. Thank you for asking."

title: Sentence Stress

revision.summary: Learn to stress the content words in a sentence (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, negatives) and reduce the small words, so your English sounds natural and clear.
examples: I WANT to BUY a new PHONE.

body_content:
Sentence Stress

English is a stress-timed language: some words are long and clear, others are short and quiet. Stressed words carry the meaning. If you stress every word equally, listeners find it hard to follow you.

1. Content words and function words

  • Content words are stressed: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, negatives, question words.
  • Function words are usually weak: articles, prepositions, auxiliaries, pronouns.

Example: I WANT to BUY a new PHONE. Read it and clap on the capital words only.

2. Rhythm

The time between stressed words stays about the same. So "Cats eat fish" and "The cats are eating the fish" take almost the same time. In the second sentence the small words are squeezed together.

3. Changing the meaning

Stress can show what is important or new. Listen: I didn't take your book. (someone else did) / I didn't TAKE your book. (I borrowed it) / I didn't take YOUR book. (I took another one).

4. Word stress in noun and verb pairs

Some two-syllable words change stress: a REcord (noun) and to reCORD (verb); a PREsent and to preSENT.

5. Where accents differ

Sentence stress works the same way in both accents. Some individual words are stressed differently:

UKadVERtisement = /ədˈvɜːtɪsmənt/
garage = /ˈɡærɑːʒ/ or /ˈɡærɪdʒ/
laboratory = /ləˈbɒrətri/
USadvertISEment = /ˌædvərˈtaɪzmənt/
garage = /ɡəˈrɑːʒ/
laboratory = /ˈlæbrətɔːri/
Practice tip: take any sentence, underline the content words, and say only those words. Then add the small words quickly between them.

title: Linking Words in Speech

revision.summary: Learn how English speakers link the end of one word to the start of the next (consonant-vowel, vowel-vowel, same consonant) so you can say and understand fast speech.

body_content:
Linking Words in Speech

In natural speech there are no gaps between words. The end of one word joins the start of the next. Learning the main links helps you speak smoothly and understand fast speakers.

1. Consonant + vowel

When a word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel, the consonant moves across: turn off sounds like "tur-noff", check in sounds like "che-kin", pick it up sounds like "pi-ki-tup".

2. Vowel + vowel

A small sound joins two vowels. After /iː/, /aɪ/, /eɪ/ it is /j/: I am = "I-y-am", she asked = "she-y-asked". After /uː/, /əʊ/ it is /w/: go on = "go-w-on", do it = "do-w-it".

3. Same consonant twice

When the same consonant sound ends one word and starts the next, say it once but a little longer: black cat, big game, some more.

4. Where accents differ

Linking is common in both accents. The difference is the "r":

UKfar away = "fah-r-away" (r appears only before a vowel)
car park = "cah park" (no r)
here it is = "here-r-it is" (linking r)
USfar away = "far away" (r is always pronounced)
car park = "car park" (r pronounced)
here it is = "here it is" (r already there)
Practice tip: write a sentence, draw a small line under each link, and say it without stops.

title: Intonation in Questions

revision.summary: Learn the rising and falling intonation of yes/no questions, wh- questions, question tags and lists, and how it shows meaning and attitude.
examples: You're coming, aren't you? (rising = asking, falling = checking)

body_content:
Intonation in Questions

Intonation is the music of your voice: it goes up and down. It shows if you are asking, checking, or being polite or bored. Listen for the pitch on the last stressed word.

1. Yes/no questions

The voice usually rises at the end: Are you ready? Do you like it? The rise shows you are waiting for an answer.

2. Wh- questions

The voice usually falls at the end: Where do you live? What time is it? A rising voice on a wh- question sounds more friendly or is used to ask for repetition: "You live WHERE?"

3. Question tags

With a rising tag you really ask: You're coming, aren't you? (I do not know.) With a falling tag you expect agreement: Nice day, isn't it?

4. Lists

In a list the voice rises on each item and falls on the last: "We need eggs (↗), milk (↗), bread (↗) and butter (↘)."

5. Where accents differ

Both accents use the patterns above. Some differences in everyday speech:

UKRight? and Yeah? at the end for checking
Polite questions often have a bigger rise
Many statements can end with a small rise in regions such as Northern Ireland
USRight? and OK? at the end for checking
Some speakers use a rising tone on statements ("uptalk")
Wh- questions usually fall
Practice tip: ask the same question two ways, rising and falling, and notice how the meaning changes.

title: Listening: Interviews

revision.summary: Practise listening to job and news interviews, catching questions, main answers and examples, with UK and US vocabulary differences.
examples: Tell me about your last job.
I've worked as a nurse for five years.

body_content:
Listening: Interviews

Interviews follow a pattern: a question, a main answer and often an example. If you follow this pattern, you can understand long answers.

1. Listening strategy

  • First listen for the question (what does the speaker want to know?).
  • Then find the main answer (it is usually in the first sentence).
  • Finally catch an example (signalled by for example, for instance, when I).

2. Script 1: a job interview

A: Tell me about your last job.
B: I've worked as a nurse for five years at a city hospital. For example, I trained new staff and organised the night shifts.
A: Why do you want to change?
B: I'd like more responsibility and to learn new skills.

Main answers: nurse, five years and more responsibility. Example: trained new staff.

3. Script 2: a radio interview

A: You've just opened a bakery. How is business?
B: Better than expected. We were busy from the first day, mainly because people heard about us online.
A: What is your plan for next year?
B: We hope to open a second shop.

Key details: better than expected, online, second shop.

4. Signal phrases

  • Mainly, mostly = the biggest reason.
  • However, but = a contrast is coming.
  • In the future, next year = a plan.

5. Where UK and US differ

UKCV = document about your career
notice period for leaving a job
holiday = time off
USresume = document about your career
two weeks' notice for leaving a job
vacation = time off
Practice tip: listen to a short interview and write the question, the main answer and one example.

title: Listening: Short Talks

revision.summary: Practise following short talks by catching the topic, the order of ideas (first, then, finally) and the main message, with UK and US differences.
examples: Today I'm going to talk about...

body_content:
Listening: Short Talks

A short talk has a beginning, a middle and an end. The speaker usually tells you the topic first and uses signal words to show the order of ideas.

1. Script 1: a talk about sleep

Today I'm going to talk about sleep. First, most adults need seven to eight hours a night. Second, screens before bed make it harder to fall asleep. Finally, a regular routine really helps. So, the main point is simple: go to bed at the same time every night.

Topic: sleep. Ideas: 7-8 hours, screens, routine. Main message: same time every night.

2. Script 2: a talk about a town

I'd like to tell you about my home town. It is small, but it has a beautiful old market. Many visitors come in summer. However, in winter it is very quiet, and that is why I love it.

Contrast word: however. The speaker's feeling: loves the quiet winter.

3. Signal words for order and contrast

  • First, second, then, next, finally = order.
  • However, but, although = contrast.
  • So, in short, the main point is = the conclusion.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKat the weekend
autumn
fortnight = two weeks
maths
USon the weekend
fall
two weeks
math
Practice tip: after listening to a talk, say the topic and three main ideas in your own words.

title: Listening: Phone Calls

revision.summary: Practise listening to phone calls, catching the reason for the call, spelled names, numbers and next steps, with UK and US phone language.
examples: Could I speak to Ms Brown, please?
I'll call you back. (UK also: ring)

body_content:
Listening: Phone Calls

On the phone you cannot see faces, so you must listen carefully. Follow four steps: who is calling, why, the key details (names, numbers, times) and the next step.

1. Script 1: making an appointment

A: Good morning, Riverside Dental.
B: Hello, I'd like to make an appointment for a check-up.
A: Certainly. Is Thursday at ten possible?
B: Could we do Friday? I'm working on Thursday.
A: Friday at eleven thirty is free.
B: Perfect. It's Carla Nunez. That's N-U-N-E-Z.

Why: check-up. Details: Friday, 11:30, name Nunez.

2. Script 2: leaving a message

A: Could I speak to Mr Hall, please?
B: I'm afraid he's in a meeting. Can I take a message?
A: Yes, please tell him Ann called about the report. My number is 0161 555 0123.
B: I'll pass that on.

Next step: Mr Hall will get the message.

3. Useful phrases

  • Speaking. = I am the person you want.
  • Hold on. / Hold the line. = wait.
  • Could you spell that, please? = ask for the spelling.
  • I'm afraid... = polite bad news.

4. Where UK and US differ

UKMr Hall (no full stop)
ring / call someone
Who's calling?
mobile
USMr. Hall (with a full stop)
call someone
Who's this?
cell phone
Practice tip: ask a friend to spell a name to you over the phone and write it down before you check.
